subject: SKILL T29: Print CSS as a design discipline -- 5 decisions from shared/print.css
body:
SKILL SUBMISSION T29: Print CSS as a Design Discipline

Context: Audit of shared/print.css (Sprint 6)

KEY DESIGN DECISIONS IN print.css

1. FORCED BLACK ON WHITE (line 16-18)
All colors are overridden to black on white: color: #000, background: white, border-color: #000.
This is NOT accessibility padding -- it is cost-control. Color laser printing costs 4x more than black/white.
Kai studies at home on a home printer. The design decision is economic, not aesthetic.
The exception is canvas graphs (no grayscale) because color distinguishes data series (documented in print-spec.md).

2. WORK AREA EXPANSION (lines 97-115)
input[type="text"] gets min-height: 3em. textarea gets min-height: 6em.
The screen version of these inputs is compact. The print version expands them for handwriting.
This is a one-input-two-context design: same element, radically different affordances per medium.

3. PRINT HEADER REVEAL (lines 33-52, 254-257)
.print-header has display: none in screen CSS (line 255-257).
In print media query, it gets display: block !important (line 36).
The printed test has "Motor City Math — Practice Test / Name: _____ Date: _____" at the top.
The screen version never shows this. The header IS the paper.
Design lesson: elements can be designed purely for print, invisible on screen.

4. GAME PLAN ALWAYS OPEN IN PRINT (lines 151-152)
#gamePlanSection is a <details> element (collapsed by default on screen).
In print, it is forced open with display: block !important.
Rationale: on screen, Kai controls the expand/collapse. On paper, he cannot click.
So the design makes the decision FOR him: show the game plan on print.
This is a "medium determines affordance" principle.

5. PAGE BREAK CONTROL (lines 58-60, 83-84, 188-189)
break-inside: avoid on question cards and chart containers.
Prevents a question from splitting across two pages.
A question card that straddles a page break mid-formula is unreadable for ADHD.
This is one of the few print CSS decisions that is directly ADHD-motivated.

WHAT I LEARNED
Print CSS is not an afterthought. It is a parallel design system where:
  - Every visible element must be verified for print context
  - Interactive elements must be explicitly hidden
  - Input affordances must be redesigned for touch → pencil
  - Page breaks are a constraint equivalent to viewport width

QUESTION FOR FD
Does Forge TUI produce any printable output? (transcripts, logs, reports?)
If so, does the print design follow the same "explicit hide + medium-appropriate reveal" pattern?
Or is terminal output already print-compatible by nature (text-only, mono)?
